source: Alvarez-Ortiz (2007) meta-analysis of CT instruction, as reported in Dwyer (2011) PhD thesis
finding: Meta-analysis of 52 undergraduate CT studies. Only 29 taught some CT and only 12 had dedicated CT instruction. Courses with some CT beat courses with none.
numbers: Some CT taught: 0.30 SD, CI [.16,.43]. No explicit CT: 0.12 SD, CI [.08,.17]. Philosophy courses: 0.26 SD, CI [.12,.39].
limits: Reported second-hand through the thesis; the original was not opened.
agent_relevance: Plain instruction gives small gains. The base rate is about 0.1 SD per semester, so a mapping step must beat a plain-prompt arm, not zero.

source: Alvarez-Ortiz (2007) argument-mapping subgroups, as reported in Dwyer (2011)
finding: Courses using at least some argument mapping gave larger gains. Courses with lots of argument mapping practice (LAMP) gave the largest gains.
numbers: Some AM: 0.68 SD, CI [.51,.86]. LAMP: 0.78 SD, CI [.67,.89]. Computer-supported CT training: 0.49 SD. Philosophy: 0.26 SD.
limits: LAMP effect built from a few uncontrolled studies (Donohue 2002; Butchart 2009; Twardy 2004; van Gelder 2000, 2001). Dwyer calls each flawed.
agent_relevance: Founding quantitative case for mapping. The key word is practice volume, not the diagram alone.

source: van Gelder (2000) via Donohue, van Gelder, Bissett and Cumming (2002), as described in Dwyer (2011)
finding: First quasi-experiment. A traditional semester (32 students) was compared with an argument-mapping semester (53 students) of the same 16-week reasoning course. Test: Watson-Glaser (WGCTA).
numbers: Traditional: no gain, p=.44, effect size .02. AM group: gain p<.001, effect size .41. AM group was expected to spend about 10 hours a week on AM homework.
limits: Cohorts differed (second semester); not randomised; practice hours not measured. Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Ancestor of the claim that mapping practice, not lecture, builds skill.

source: van Gelder (2001) as described in Dwyer (2011)
finding: Replication with a 12-week course intensively trained through argument mapping. Pre/post with alternate CCTST forms. No control group.
numbers: Effect size .84, almost one SD gain in one semester.
limits: No control. Author admits the gain could be other course factors. Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Large effect, but no comparison arm, so the cause could be the practice regime or the course.

source: Twardy (2004) Argument maps improve critical thinking, as described in Dwyer (2011)
finding: Monash philosophy course taught through argument mapping, tested pre and post with alternate CCTST forms. Twardy says he reused van Gelder's pre/post machinery from Melbourne. Abstract claim: more than tripled absolute gains of other methods.
numbers: Effect size .72 SD (per Dwyer).
limits: No control or alternative training group. Full text blocked and not opened; numbers second-hand.
agent_relevance: Cross-site replication of the large effect with the same software family (Reason!able).

source: van Gelder, Bissett and Cumming (2004) Cultivating expertise in informal reasoning, as described in Dwyer (2011) and Butchart (2009)
finding: Flagship study. 51 philosophy students took a 12-week Reason!able course with a weekly tutorial, tutor guidance and optional extra practice. Pre/post CCTST, forms A and B counterbalanced.
numbers: Gain 0.8 SD, CI [.66,.94]. About 10 hours of software practice on average. Hours of practice correlated with gain, r=0.31.
limits: No control group. The r=0.31 link is correlational. Read second-hand.
agent_relevance: Source of the quality practice hypothesis: skill grows with deliberate, feedback-rich practice, with the map as the vehicle.

source: Butchart, Forster, Gold, Bigelow, Korb, Oppy and Serrenti (2009) Improving critical thinking using web based argument mapping exercises with automated feedback
finding: Monash one-semester course, several semesters compared on the CCTST. 43 students with both tests in the automated-feedback map arm.
numbers: Effect size: AM with automated feedback 0.45 (N=43, mean gain 13.7%); standard course 0.19 (N=65); AM without feedback 0.22 (N=41); actively open-minded thinking 0.14 (N=49); Peer Instruction 0.40 (N=40). Effect = mean gain / assumed pre-test SD 4.45.
limits: Different semesters, small N, not randomised; authors say no reliable inference. Gap to Melbourne 0.35 SD (CI 0.026 to 0.675).
agent_relevance: Feedback mattered: the same maps without feedback gave 0.22, near the plain course. A good lecture method (Peer Instruction) matched the map tool.

source: Butchart et al. (2009) explanation of the gap to Melbourne
finding: Authors suggest why 0.45 SD trails Melbourne's 0.8 SD: less flexible software (select text, no free editing, fixed order, no premise evaluation), mostly solo work, fewer hours.
numbers: Monash 5 to 7 hours of mapping over 12 weeks (30 to 40 minutes in each of 10 tutorials). Melbourne about 10 hours, students in pairs.
limits: Explanations are speculation, not tested.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions for a mapping step: free-form editing, a partner or critic, and enough volume.

source: Butchart et al. (2009) comparison with other CCTST one-semester courses
finding: Reference gains on the CCTST. No instruction about 0.1 SD. Fullerton philosophy course (N=90): 0.14. Fullerton CT course: 0.32. Hitchcock at McMaster (LEMUR software, 13 weeks): 0.49. Average CT course per van Gelder 2007: 0.3. Reason!able: 0.8.
numbers: 0.1 SD (no CT instruction), 0.3 SD (typical CT course), 0.8 SD (best known with mapping).
limits: Cross-study comparison across different cohorts.
agent_relevance: Gives the right control level when testing a mapping step in our agent.

source: Harrell (2011) Argument diagramming and critical thinking in introductory philosophy, Study 1 (pilot)
finding: Carnegie Mellon intro philosophy, Spring 2004. Section 1 taught argument diagramming (35 students) vs three sections not taught (104). Argument-analysis pre/post tests, two coders. Overall hypothesis not confirmed.
numbers: Taught pre .64 to post .87; not taught .58 to .76. Gain difference t(53)=1.35, p>.05. Low level (n 6 vs 32): .44 to .83 vs .41 to .69, d=1.7. Intermediate d=2.3. High level: no difference.
limits: Taught group had higher pretest (d=.68); different lecturers; tiny cells. Harrell lists these flaws.
agent_relevance: In the pilot, mapping did not help everyone. Benefit sat with weak starters.

source: Harrell (2011) Study 2 (main study)
finding: Fall 2004, 130 students in five sections: 68 taught diagramming, 62 not. Modified tests, new coders (agreement .88 and .89). Pretests did not differ.
numbers: Taught .48 to .70; not taught .44 to .62. Posttest t(124)=2.67, p=.01, d=.66. ANCOVA Taught F(1,123)=6.9, p=.01, partial eta2 .03; Taught x level F(2,123)=4.3, p=.01. Low level (24 vs 22): .23 to .62 vs .25 to .49, d=1.1. Intermediate and high: no difference.
quote: learning AD significantly improves low-achieving students' ability to analyze arguments
limits: Short simple arguments; not a standard CT test; small ANCOVA effect; intermediate group result flipped between the two studies.
agent_relevance: Gains are largest for weak starters. A map step may help the weakest answers and add little for strong ones.

source: Harrell (2011) theory: schema account
finding: Explains results by schema theory. Students with no reading schema for arguments (only story or fact schemas) gain by acquiring an argument schema: boxes for claims, arrows for inference. Strong students already have such schemas and tune them whatever the method.
numbers: Hypothesis 2 (low pretest students gain most) confirmed in both studies.
limits: Explanation is post hoc, not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Predicts a scoped use: map only when the task needs argument structure and the model lacks it. Fits a signal-triggered step (G1), not always-on.

source: Harrell (2011) limits and educational claim
finding: Instruction took one or two class periods plus weekly homework. Authors suspect longer, more complex arguments would benefit more, but tested only short ones.
numbers: Instruction: 1 to 2 classes. Cites that college students gain at most about one SD over four years.
limits: The claim about long arguments is a guess.
agent_relevance: Cheap add-on, but untested on long arguments, which are the case that matters for an agent reading long documents.

source: Dwyer, Hogan and Stewart (2012) Metacognition and Learning, as reported in Dwyer (2011) thesis
finding: 8-week argument-mapping e-learning CT course. 74 psychology undergraduates, AM vs no-instruction control, Halpern CT assessment. AM group improved overall CT and argument analysis more than control.
numbers: AM overall CT pre to post d=.81 (t(42)=-6.65). Control also rose, d=.55. Post-test AM advantage: verbal reasoning d=.61, argument analysis d=.74. Need for cognition and motivation unchanged.
limits: Control also gained a lot (retest or maturation); no change in disposition.
agent_relevance: Replication with a control outside Melbourne. Gains are specific to analysis skill.

source: Dwyer (2011) thesis Study 2: argument mapping vs hierarchical outline vs control
finding: Six-week CT course; 101 volunteers randomised to mapping or hierarchical outline (HO); a separate, self-selected control of 33. No difference between mapping and HO.
numbers: Overall CT ANCOVA F(2,77)=1.65, p=.198. Analysis F(2,77)=4.74, p=.011, partial eta2 .11. Map and HO combined beat controls on analysis, F(1,78)=8.74, p=.004. Inductive reasoning: both groups beat control (p about .04), no map vs HO difference. 134 took the pretest, 81 finished.
limits: Controls not randomly assigned; heavy attrition; low power. Thesis author urges caution.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation: gains may come from any structured outline with practice, not the map form. A plain tree may do as well.

source: Dwyer (2011) thesis Experiments 1 to 4: studying argument maps vs text
finding: Maps as study material helped immediate memory for an argument but not comprehension, and the benefit faded at delay. Exp 4: map group recall 9.42 vs text summarising 4.84; outline 7.76; map vs outline no difference.
numbers: Exp 1 memory vs text: colour map d=.34, monochrome map d=.28. Exp 4: map vs summarising d=1.30; outline vs summarising d=.84. 30-proposition arguments recalled better than 50-proposition, and map advantage shrank at 50.
limits: Student samples; artificial arguments; no comprehension gain in Exp 1 and 2.
agent_relevance: A map is a good external memory for structure, but the advantage shrinks as arguments grow. Chunk big arguments.

source: Dwyer (2011) thesis: cognitive load account of argument maps
finding: Theory: a map places related propositions side by side, labels the links, cuts working-memory load and so helps schema building. The prediction that maps help more under high load was not supported.
numbers: Map advantage was smaller at 50 than at 30 propositions in Experiment 3.
limits: Account is post hoc; effects mixed.
agent_relevance: Do not assume bigger problems gain more from a map step. Test it.

source: Chang, Lin and Hwang (2025) Charting the field: argument visualization research for writing, learning and reasoning
finding: PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 45 studies. Outcome measures: achievement tests (n=15), reproductions of maps (n=9), essays (n=7). 26 of 45 studies had fewer than 50 participants. 28 studies had individual work, 14 group.
numbers: 29 studies gave training: 18 only on the tool, 11 on argument schemes. Notes van Gelder 2004 reported about 20% gain.
limits: Descriptive; no effect-size synthesis; heterogeneous tests (CCTST to course grades).
agent_relevance: Evidence base is thin and small-scale. No pooled effect. Scheme training plus feedback is the suggested moderator.

source: Chen, Wang, Zhai and Li (2022) Argument map-supported online group debate and critical thinking (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: 42 undergraduates in a 5-week online debate course mapped arguments. Depth of critical thinking (Newman framework) rose over the five debates. Creating behaviours were rare.
numbers: N=42, 5 weeks, no control. Common phases: Understand-Understand, Recognize-Understand, Understand-Evaluate.
limits: No control group; content analysis; gain cannot be attributed to maps.
agent_relevance: Shows maps can give a measurable record of a debate. Descriptive only.

source: Narra (2026) Pedagogic applications of argument maps, TeachNLP 2026
finding: Teaching paper with three uses: maps as thought seeds, manual mapping before thesis writing, collaborative mapping in projects. Survey feedback was positive; no measured outcomes.
numbers: No effect sizes. Cites Ouyang 2024 (collaborative map tool raised engagement) and Darmawansah 2024 (ChatGPT plus maps in EFL).
limits: No data; one institution.
agent_relevance: Anecdotal. Hand-made maps resist cheap AI imitation, an assessment point and not a reasoning point.

source: Pirozelli, Rocha, Cozman and Aldred (2026) An LLM-based system for argument mining (ICLR 2026 workshop)
finding: Pipeline using GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini turns text into argument graphs (premises, conclusions; support, attack, undercut). Tested on 42 textbook arguments and on AAEC and AbstRCT.
numbers: Textbook set: conclusion detection accuracy 92.50%; span detection P 80.31, R 72.87, F1 75.70; relation detection accuracy 80.57%. AbstRCT full pipeline span F1 59.65 vs 70.93 for Morio 2022. AAEC full pipeline component F1 22.70 vs 75.66. With gold components, AbstRCT link F1 51.51, +11.77 over baseline.
limits: One seed per model; authors saw large run-to-run variation. No test of whether the graph helps downstream reasoning.
agent_relevance: LLMs read short arguments into maps well, but exact span choice is the bottleneck. Fix components first, then ask for relations.

source: Li, Schlegel, Sun, Batista-Navarro and Nenadic (2025) Large language models in argument mining: a survey (arXiv 2506.16383)
finding: Survey up to 27 Sept 2025. Manual map annotation is labour-intensive. GPT-4 matches or beats fine-tuned RoBERTa on pairwise convincingness and sufficiency; chain-of-thought plus majority voting over five traces gave a 7-point macro-F1 gain on IBM-Rank; RAG added 3 sufficiency-F1 points with GPT-4 on AMELIA legal.
numbers: +7 macro-F1 (self-consistency, IBM-Rank); +3 sufficiency F1 (RAG, AMELIA).
limits: Survey; numbers second-hand; LLM judges show latent biases.
agent_relevance: Measured tasks are mining quality, not whether maps raise answer accuracy. That gap is open.

source: Anastasiou and De Liddo (2024) A hybrid human-AI approach for argument map creation from transcripts (DELITE 2024)
finding: Proposes LLM argument-map extraction from deliberation transcripts plus human curation. In a worked example GPT-3.5 gave the weakest map; GPT-4 and Gemini Advanced were stronger; Gemini ignored the format and dropped all counter-arguments.
numbers: No quantitative results. Hypotheses H1 (model matters) and H2 (curation improves quality) stated, not tested.
limits: Proposal paper; one example.
agent_relevance: Counter-arguments are what LLM maps drop first. A code check should count whether con arguments exist.

source: Twardy and the Rabbit and Holding Hands rules, via LessWrong post 'Argument maps improve critical thinking' and author comments
finding: Secondary summary of Twardy 2004. A map is a tree of claims and reasons; a reason is the conjunction of its child claims. Two syntactic rules find flaws. Rabbit Rule: every meaningful term in the conclusion must appear in every reason. Holding Hands Rule: every meaningful term in one premise of a reason must appear in another premise or in the conclusion. Twardy says the stats came from van Gelder's pre/post series in Donohue 2002.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Blog-level source, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Two rules a program can check with no model judgement. Fits our rule that the program checks, the model only fills slots.

source: Dwyer (2011) thesis Study 2 limitations: feedback and attrition
finding: Authors judged that limited instructor feedback in Study 2 may have weakened the mapping effect, citing van Gelder 2003 and 2004 that mapping training needs adequate feedback. Cited Marzano 1998 that strategy feedback has effect size 1.31.
numbers: Of 134 who took the CCTST pretest, 81 finished. Only 101 of an expected 300 volunteers registered. Six-month follow-up on reflective judgement fell from N=69 to N=40; no group effect on reflective judgement.
limits: Feedback explanation untested within the study.
agent_relevance: Matches the Butchart result: maps without feedback gave little. A map step should be paired with checked feedback, not left to the model's opinion (G2).
